title: What time is it?
goal: Tell the time and the day, talk about your work schedule — and fit in the biggest verb group, the one ending in *-a*, with its two patterns: plain and with the *-ez* insert.
bekal: ask and tell the time: *și un sfert, și jumătate, fără un sfert*, and *la* + time
conjugate *-a* verbs in both patterns: *cânt* versus *lucrez*
name the days and parts of the day, and tell *sâmbătă* (this Saturday) from *sâmbăta* (every Saturday)

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Dimineața, în bucătărie
dialogs.intro: Morning in the apartment kitchen. Andrei has just woken up and is still looking for his phone; Budi already has his keys in hand, about to leave for the office.

lines.speaker: Andrei:
lines.text: Bună dimineața, Budi! Cât este ceasul?
lines.id: Good morning, Budi! What time is it?
lines.literal: good-f morning-the, Budi! how-much it-is clock-the?

lines.speaker: Andrei:
lines.text: Deja? La ce oră începi lucrul?
lines.id: Already? What time do you start work?
lines.literal: already? at what hour you-start work-the?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Încep la nouă. Și tu? La ce oră începe cursul?
lines.id: I start at nine. And you? What time does your class start?
lines.literal: I-start at nine. and you? at what hour it-starts course-the?

lines.speaker: Andrei:
lines.text: La zece și jumătate. Am timp. Lucrezi în fiecare zi?
lines.id: At half past ten. I've got time. Do you work every day?
lines.literal: at ten and half. I-have time. you-work in every day?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Lucrez de luni până vineri. Sâmbăta nu lucrez.
lines.id: I work from Monday to Friday. On Saturdays I don't work.
lines.literal: I-work from Monday until Friday. Saturday-the not I-work.

lines.speaker: Andrei:
lines.id: And where do you eat at lunchtime?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: La prânz mănânc la unu, cu colegii.
lines.id: At lunchtime I eat at one, with my colleagues.
lines.literal: at noon I-eat at one, with colleagues-the.

lines.speaker: Andrei:
lines.text: Eu mănânc acasă. Iar seara cânt într-o trupă.
lines.id: I eat at home. And in the evenings I sing in a band.
lines.literal: I I-eat at-home. and evening-the I-sing in-a-f band.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Seriously? And when do you play?

lines.speaker: Andrei:
lines.text: Vineri seara, la opt și jumătate, în Centrul Vechi. Ești liber?
lines.id: Friday evening, at half past eight, in Centrul Vechi. Are you free?
lines.literal: Friday evening-the, at eight and half, in center-the old. you-are free?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Da, vineri seara sunt liber. Oh, e deja opt și douăzeci! Pa!
lines.id: Yes, I'm free on Friday evening. Oh, it's already twenty past eight! Bye!
lines.literal: yes, Friday evening-the I-am free. oh, it-is already eight and twenty! bye!

notes: **Cât este ceasul?** literally "how much is the clock?" — *ceas* is the object: a watch, a clock. Another question that's just as common: *Ce oră este?* and, more casually, *Cât e ceasul?* The answer always opens with *Este…* or *E…*

**La nouă, la unu, la zece și jumătate.** "At such-and-such a time" is always *la* + number; the word *ora* can be said (*la ora nouă*) or not. *Zece și jumătate* = ten **and** a half = 10:30, just like English "half past ten" (not German *halb zehn*, which is 9:30). Romanian counts forward from the hour that has passed.

**Începi lucrul.** *Lucru* (n) means "work", and since it ends in *-u* it just takes *-l*: *lucrul* — the rule from unit 4. The verb is *a începe* (to begin): *încep, începi, începe, începem, începeți, încep*. It belongs to the *-e* group, which gets sorted out in unit 8.

**De luni până vineri. Sâmbăta nu lucrez.** Day names need no preposition: *vineri seara* = (on) Friday evening. But once they take the definite article, the meaning becomes a **habit**: *sâmbăta* = on Saturdays, *seara* = in the evenings. One letter *-a* replaces "every" — like English *on Saturday* versus *on Saturdays*.

**Într-o trupă, cu colegii.** *În* can't stand right before *un/o*; it stretches into *într-un, într-o*: *într-o trupă, într-un parc*. And *cu colegii* shows two things from unit 6 at once: the masculine plural article *-ii*, and *cu* as the one preposition that keeps the article.

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: The pattern is simple: the first half of the hour counts **forward** with *și* (and), the second half counts **back** from the next hour with *fără* (without, to). *Un sfert* = a quarter, *jumătate* = half.

head: Time
Română
Literally
rows: it is (the hour) eight / eight sharp
the hour one · the hour two

after: **The hour is feminine — almost always.** Because *oră* is a feminine noun, numbers with two forms use the feminine one: *ora **două***, *ora **douăsprezece***, *douăzeci și **două***. The one rebel is the number one: the standard form is *ora **unu***, not *ora una*. Just memorize it: *la unu, la două*.

**Morning or evening?** In conversation people use 1–12 and add the part of the day when needed: *la opt dimineața* (8 a.m.), *la opt seara* (8 p.m.), *la trei după-amiaza* (3 p.m.). Train timetables, cinemas, and official announcements use the 24-hour clock: *șaptesprezece și treizeci* = 17:30.
Handy little words around the clock: *fix* (sharp), *aproape* (almost — *e aproape nouă*), *deja* (already), *de la… până la…* (from… to…): *de la nouă până la cinci*.

grammars.title: Verbs ending in -a: two patterns
body: The *-a* group is the largest, and every new verb that enters Romanian joins it. It splits in two: some verbs attach the ending straight to the stem, others slip in ***-ez*** first — like *-esc* in *vorbesc* in unit 2. *A mânca* (to eat) follows the plain pattern, but its stem changes slightly.
after: **The "he/she" and "they" forms are always twins** in this group: *el cântă, ei cântă*; *ea lucrează, ele lucrează*. That's why *costă* in unit 5 works for one ticket or ten.

**The *-ez* insert appears only in four forms** — *eu, tu, el/ea, ei/ele*. The *noi* and *voi* forms are always plain: *lucrăm, lucrați*, never *lucrezăm*. The same happens with *a mânca*: the long stem *mănânc-* in those four forms, the short stem *mânc-* in *noi* and *voi*.

**Which verbs take *-ez*?** You can't tell from the infinitive; that's why this book's vocabulary always gives the *eu* form in brackets. With the insert: *a lucra (lucrez), a traversa (traversez), a studia (studiez), a vizita (vizitez), a dansa (dansez)*. Plain: *a cânta (cânt), a asculta (ascult), a întreba (întreb), a ajuta (ajut), a pleca (plec), a cumpăra (cumpăr)*.
Notice *cânți*: the *-i* ending softens *t* into *ț*, just like *student → studenți* in unit 5. The same sound change works in nouns and verbs — learn it once, use it twice.

blocks.text: Day names are written in **lowercase** and are all feminine. Without the article they point to one particular day: *Vineri sunt liber* (I'm free this Friday). With the article they become a habit: *Vinerea cânt într-o trupă* (on Fridays I sing in a band). Time words that go with them: *azi* (today), *mâine* (tomorrow), *ieri* (yesterday), *în weekend* (at the weekend), *în fiecare zi* (every day), *săptămâna aceasta* (this week).

blocks.title: Where the day names come from
items: The five working days are named after Roman heavenly bodies and gods, inherited straight from Latin: *luni* (Luna, the moon), *marți* (Mars), *miercuri* (Mercury), *joi* (Jupiter), *vineri* (Venus). If you've ever studied Spanish, French, or Italian, you'll recognize them all.

*Sâmbătă* comes from "sabbath" — and *duminică* means "the Lord's day", from Latin *dominica*, like Spanish *domingo*. English took its day names from Norse and Saxon gods instead, but *Monday* (moon day) and *luni* are still the same idea.
The week in Romania starts on **Monday**; wall calendars are printed starting from *luni*.

blocks.text: Just like day names, parts of the day **with the article** stand alone without a preposition and mean "at that time, usually": *Dimineața lucrez acasă. După-amiaza studiez româna. Seara ascult muzică. Noaptea nu lucrez.* Only *prânz* needs *la*. And because *seara* starts around six o'clock, Romanians already say *Bună seara!* at the time an English speaker might still say "good afternoon".

blocks.title: Program: opening hours on the shop door
items: The word ***Program*** on the door of a shop, bank, or pharmacy isn't a show — it's the **opening hours**. Days are abbreviated *L, Ma, Mi, J, V, S, D*; so *L–V 9–18* means Monday to Friday, nine to six.
*Deschis* = open, *închis* = closed. Many small shops close early on Saturdays and stay shut on Sundays, so don't leave your shopping until *duminică*.
A ***Non-Stop*** sign marks a small shop or pharmacy open 24 hours — a lifesaver if, like Budi, you only remember dinner close to midnight.
